newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW -- U.S. Q2 ECI rises 0.8 pct.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW -- U.S. Q2 ECI rises 0.8 pct.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Labor Department said the Employment Cost Index (ECI) rose 0.8 percent in the second quarter compared to a 0.6-percent rise in the first three months of the year.
Economists in a Reuters survey had expected a 0.8-percent rise in second quarter ECI.
JOHN LONSKI, SENIOR ECONOMIST, MOODY'S INVESTORS SERVICE INC: "I think the market of course was looking for a lower-than-expected reading.

"I think we're probably looking at ... underlying medical care costs of about 3.0 percent," Lonski added. Costs of benefits overall rose 0.6 percent in the second quarter compared to a mere 0.1-percent increase in the prior period.
Lonski was speaking on Reuters Financial Television.

NICK PERNA, CHIEF ECONOMIST, FLEET BANK: "It's pretty much in line with expectations. It's not cause for concern. Anything larger would have raised fears of not just impending, but actual inflation. This is one important hurdle that we've cleared for the week."

DAN SETO, SENIOR ECONOMIST, THE NIKKO SECURITIES CO INTERNATIONAL INC: "The report is actually fairly serene in terms of inflation pressures. The assessment after this number is that the economy is about where we thought it would be. Wages and salaries remained within this trend. We have seen some rebound in benefits costs."

KEVIN FLANAGAN, MONEY MARKET ECONOMIST AND VICE PRESIDENT, DEAN WITTER REYNOLDS INC: "It was in line with expectations. The (bond) market initially came of a little bit, but this figure shouldn't present a problem.
"Benefit costs have been held in check; there just had been some problems with the way the (Bureau of Labor Statistics) measured them, particulary in the transportation sector," he added.

GARY THAYER, SENIOR ECONOMIST, A.G. EDWARDS & SONS INC: "It's a good number. It shows the costs of workers to firms are still relatively restrained. Wages are up, but benefits are rising much more slowly, allowing companies, as we've seen over the last year, to hire more workers.
